I like this variant where you call out what users will learn more about. I think it's nice to bring "protect your privacy" up front.
Rationale for adding "for Review Checker" to the settings thing? I think it works in context of sidebar without it. @Katie Lower

Is there a version that could combine the hypothesis version + this one? 

Show relevant ads
* Ads you see in Review Checker aren't based on personal data, just anonymized click data. [LINK] Learn how we protect your privacy
I like how simple this is. If you "trust" Firefox, this should suffice. If you're skeptical, learn more is right there
I do like the funny approach! :joy: Nice use of voice.

global comment...

I'm hesitant to use the word "relevant" because

1) relevant could make you feel like they are more based on my data or history (especially if they don't feel actually relevant. e.g. "keyword triggers product not relevant to the page"

2) as we do improve relevance for these ads, there could be an opportunity to call that out later. harder to notice the change if we already call them "relevant"

RIFFS

"Show related ads"
"Show ads"
"Show ads in Review Checker"
"Show sponsored products"

With a headline that says "show relevant ads" but then follow up with "we don't share your personal data" I don't think it connects the dots for me. 

I'd def ask myself "well then how am I seeing relevant ads?" So I'm leaning more towards some of the versions below that mention anon click data/not personal data.
Should it be Firefox or Review Checker as the noun? @Katie Lower
SS: If you go with a sentence link, you could shorten to "how we protect your privacy."
I think this one is my fave. Short and speaks to consumer benefit. I lean towards agreeing with Emanuela, you don't need the "Don't worry." @Katie Lower
OPO: reading "don't worry" kinda makes me worry :grimacing:

I think the "just the facts" is super easy to understand. If it's "not enough" what about combining it with another like "Firefox doesn't share your personal data with advertisers, so our ads will never follow you around the internet."
the "Don't worry" sounds a bit patronizing
This one is very effective, I like the long link
I like this one because it's straight to fact that yes, we do share something but we don't share your personal data.

@Emanuela Damiani - Exploring strings over here. Not all of them are realistic. Let me know if there are any you really like or really hate. 

I"ll be bringing these to our content critique tmrw for more feedback.

@Ekaterina Galetski here we could keep the RC inner view as-is. 

But let me know if you think we need to write new annotations for a refresher work (if this is planned).

@Ekaterina Galetski Here we could use the current pattern with the `aria-busy` being used on the inner RC container (the one below the header and Close button, which is loading here). But if possible, we could improve it by moving the "aria-busy" attribute to the general RC view (item #1 in this comment). This would ensure it is announcing the new loaded content more reliably because the general container would be always present while the inner views are changing from the opt-in to the RC results and their errors)

Focus order:
1. "X" (label: "Close", role: "button") - reference
2. "Learn more" (label: [use on-screen string], role: link).
3. "Try Review Checker" (label: [use on-screen string], role: button).
4. "privacy notice" (label: [use on-screen string], role: link).
5. "terms of use" (label: [use on-screen string], role: link).

Screen reader annotations:
1. (the whole Review Checker view, reuse the GenAI pattern for A, minus the background part of the note, of course)
2. "Review Checker Beta" (the header, likely H2 or H3 - reuse the GenAI pattern for B)
3. [TBD - we could follow the GenAI inner region role and note, or we could reuse the existent structure of the Review Checker]
4. Image - ideally, we would provide an alt text for it (mark it as informative - eng guidance included) so assistive technology users could also benefit from the emotional foxy support as sighted users do, i.e. "A fox holding a magnifying glass" or "A fox researching the reviews with a magnifying glass" or anything else - this is up to the content designers. Otherwise, the image should be marked up as decorative (the link includes detailed eng guides).
5. "Can you trust these reviews?" role: heading (visually appears like H3 but could be H2 or H4, depending on the DOM structure/heading hierarchy around, basically, should be a level down from the "Review Checker Beta" heading in the item #2 above)
6. Paragraph that includes the "Learn more" link (currently it is a heading, which we need to fix)
7. Paragraph that includes two other links. Not a bug but possible improvement idea: we could refer to this paragraph via "aria-describedby" from the "Try Review Checker" button - this would ensure a screen reader would announce the terms disclosure here when the button is focused (in case the user would not continue reviewing the page, they still would be clearly indicated that it is, in fact, a Mozilla service and not some third-party injection of sorts). @Ekaterina Galetski - WDYT?

Label: Review Checker [the name of the tool]
Role: Button/toolbarbutton
State: pressed/not pressed (via "aria-pressed" property on a <button> or "selected" on <toolbarbutton> - follow the general sidebar guidance: https://www.figma.com/design/ZFavpnAJee39j2mFf8U3D0/Sidebar-UX-Spec?node-id=7749-195365&t=lpWL1RSfbROZ8dvO-4)
@Ekaterina Galetski For this mockup and the one with the collapsed sidebar on the right, we'd need to reuse the general sidebar a11y guidance (no changes).
